title: Opinions and Feelings
description: Say what you think and how you feel without starting a fight: أظن إن, برأيي, the agree/disagree pair, and the feeling words the Gulf actually uses — مستانس, معصب, طفران — plus the softeners that let you disagree with an elder and keep the coffee coming.
approach: Authentic video with scaffolding — reaction clips and light debates, paused on every opinion verb, then a two-sided mini-debate where you must disagree politely at least twice.
unlock_condition: Give an opinion with أظن إن, agree and disagree with a softener, and name four feelings; ≥8/10 on the feelings quiz
can_do: Give your opinion and agree or disagree politely
Say how you feel and why
Say you like or hate something

grammar.title: أظن إن…: opinion verbs and the little word إن
grammar.explanation: To report a thought, the Gulf puts a small إن (that) between the opinion verb and the sentence: أظن إن المطعم غالي (I think the restaurant is expensive). إن takes a pronoun ending when the next word is a pronoun — أظن إنه مسافر، أحس إنك تعبان — and stays bare before a noun. The same إن follows أحس (I feel), أعتقد (I believe), أتوقع (I expect), قال (he said) and even ما أدري (ما أدري إذا… for 'whether'). In fast speech the إن is sometimes dropped: أظن راح. برأيي (in my opinion) needs no إن — it just sits at the front. Trap: the MSA أن with fatha and a following accusative are gone; it is one flat inn.

examples.english: I think the film is good
I feel you're upset with me
In my opinion, work starts far too early
He said he'll come after sunset prayer
I don't know whether he agrees

culture.title: Disagree with the person's point, never with the person
culture.note: In a majlis you can hold any opinion about football, cars or restaurants, but you do not contradict an elder flat out and you do not let a friend lose face. The move is to agree first — معك حق (you're right), صح (true) — then turn with بس (but) and add your view as a feeling, not a fact: بس أحس إن… (but I feel that…). بصراحة (frankly) announces that you are about to be honest and buys you permission for it; مع احترامي (with respect) is the polite way to say no to someone senior. Topics to leave alone with people you do not know well: rulers, religion between sects, and other people's wives.

phrases.english: You're right, but I feel that…

vocabulary.teaching_note: Followed by إن and a sentence. The ظ is the heavy Gulf dh and the n is doubled: a-ẔINN. Also أعتقد (I believe) and, very commonly, أحس (I feel) for the same job. Written اظن online.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman with a finger to her temple, a thought bubble containing a small restaurant.

example.english: I think the restaurant is closed today

vocabulary.video_hint: Opinion vlogs: أظن إن / أعتقد إن before a judgement.

vocabulary.teaching_note: رأي (opinion) with بـ and 'my'. Changes with the person: برأيك (in your opinion — also the question 'what do you think?'), برأيه. Sits at the front of the sentence with no إن.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man tapping his own chest and pointing at a car, a small speech bubble with a star rating.

example.english: In my opinion, winter is nicer than summer

vocabulary.video_hint: برأيي / برأيك؟ in debates and review clips.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A participle used as a whole reply: موافق؟ — موافق. Feminine موافقة, plural موافقين. The verb أوافق exists but the participle is what people say. The warmer agreement is معك حق (you're right).
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men shaking hands across a café table, both nodding.

example.english: Shall we go at five? — Agreed

vocabulary.video_hint: A deal or a plan being sealed with موافق / موافقين.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The verb with ما: ما أوافق عليك (I don't agree with you). Softer options: مو معك (I'm not with you on this) and مع احترامي. Blunt disagreement with an elder is avoided — see the culture note.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman shaking her head gently with one palm raised, still smiling.

example.english: With respect, I don't agree with you

vocabulary.video_hint: A polite objection in a debate: مو موافق / ما أوافق.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf's own word for being happy in the moment: مستانس بالسفرة (having a great time on the trip). فرحان is 'glad' about news; مبسوط is understood but sounds imported. Feminine مستانسة, plural مستانسين; the verb is أستانس.
vocabulary.image_scene: Friends around a campfire in the desert, one clapping, all laughing.

example.english: I'm having a great time on the desert trip

vocabulary.video_hint: Outing vlogs: مستانسين! said to camera.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From 'nerves' (أعصاب): معصب is angry in the everyday Gulf sense, stronger than زعلان (upset). Feminine معصبة. ليش معصب؟ (why are you angry?). زعلان is what you say about a sulking friend; معصب is a boss.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a red face and clenched fists standing over a dented car bumper.

example.english: My dad has been angry since morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Skits with an angry character: معصب / لا تعصب.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf word for restless boredom — طفران، ما عندي شي أسويه. Feminine طفرانة. The MSA ملل gives ملل (boredom) but nobody says أشعر بالملل; they say طفران. Related: طفر (to get fed up).
vocabulary.image_scene: A teenager sprawled on a sofa staring at the ceiling, phone face down on his chest.

example.english: I'm bored, come on let's go out

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone declaring طفران before suggesting an outing.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Worried about someone or something: قلقان عليك (worried about you). Two hard g sounds. The idiom شايل هم (carrying worry) is warmer; متوتر is 'tense / nervous' before an exam.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother at a window at night, holding a phone and biting her lip.

example.english: My mum is worried about me because I'm late

vocabulary.video_hint: قلقان / لا تقلق in family scenes and before results.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The thing does the liking in Arabic: يعجبني (it pleases me), تعجبني السيارة (I like the car, feminine), يعجبونني (I like them). Past عجبني. Use أحب for people and for habits; يعجبني for things you judge.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man giving a thumbs-up at a phone screen in a shop, the salesman smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: Review clips: يعجبني / ما عجبني about a product or a place.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Strong but common: أكره الزحمة (I hate traffic). Also مو حاب (not keen on) for milder dislike, and ما أطيق (I can't stand). Past كرهت.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman grimacing at a plate of okra, pushing it away with one finger.

example.english: I hate the heat and the humidity

vocabulary.video_hint: Complaints: أكره… said with feeling in vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Both physical and mental feeling: أحس بصداع (I feel a headache), أحس إنك تعبان (I feel you're tired). The Gulf's softest opinion verb — أحس إن is how you disagree gently. Doubled s: aḥiss.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a hand on his heart, a mixed sun-and-cloud symbol above his head.

example.english: I feel the weather is going to change

vocabulary.video_hint: أحس إن as an opinion opener in reaction videos.

vocabulary.teaching_note: وش رأيك؟ / شرايك؟ (what do you think?) is the question that opens every opinion exchange. Kuwaitis fuse it to شرايك. Plural آراء. Written راي / رايك online.
vocabulary.image_scene: A speech bubble with a question mark facing a speech bubble with a light bulb.

example.english: What do you think of the new restaurant?

vocabulary.video_hint: وش رأيك / شرايك؟ asked to camera or to a guest.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Announces honesty and softens what follows. Also الصراحة (the truth is…) at the front of a sentence. The ص colours the vowels dark: b-ṣa-RAA-ḥa.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman leaning in over a table, one hand flat on it, speaking earnestly.
vocabulary.video_hint: بصراحة before a verdict in reviews and reaction clips.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Wrong as an idea or an act: هذا غلط (that's wrong), رقم غلط (wrong number). Its opposite is صح. As a noun it is 'a mistake' — غلطة for one specific slip.
vocabulary.image_scene: A red X drawn over a wrong turn on a map, the correct arrow beside it.

example.english: The answer is wrong, try again

vocabulary.video_hint: Correction moments: غلط / غلطان in quizzes and arguments.

vocabulary.teaching_note: One word for 'correct' and 'true': صح؟ (right?) is the tag question after any statement. Kuwaitis also say صج, Saudis صدق, for 'really / true'. Doubled ḥ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A green tick beside a maths sum on a whiteboard.
vocabulary.video_hint: صح؟ as a tag; صح! as a reply.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'with you is right'. Changes for the person: معج حق (to a woman, east of Saudi), معكم حق. The agreement that precedes a polite disagreement: معك حق، بس…
vocabulary.image_scene: An older man nodding and raising his coffee cup slightly toward a younger speaker.

example.english: You're right, the market is expensive

vocabulary.video_hint: معك حق / عندك حق as a concession in dialogue.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The thing is ممل, the person is طفران — do not confuse them. فيلم ممل، دوام ممل. Feminine مملة.
vocabulary.image_scene: An audience yawning in a cinema, one person checking a phone.

example.english: The film was boring, I fell asleep

vocabulary.video_hint: ممل as a verdict in reviews.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Hurt, sad or sulking: زعلان مني؟ (are you upset with me?). Feminine زعلانة. The verb زعل; the fixer is لا تزعل (don't be upset).
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy sitting on the stairs with his back to the room, arms crossed.

example.english: Don't be upset, I didn't mean it

vocabulary.video_hint: زعلان / لا تزعل in family and friend scenes.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Physically and mentally: مرتاح بالشغل (happy at work), الكرسي مرتاح (the chair is comfortable). Feminine مرتاحة. Also the reply to 'how do you feel now?' after illness.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man reclining on majlis cushions with a tea glass, eyes half closed.

example.english: Are you comfortable in the new house?

vocabulary.video_hint: مرتاح as an answer about a job, a house or a car.

dialogue.transliteration: maʿich ḥagg. w-aẕinn innah ghaali baʿad

dialogue.english: Haha, I feel at ease today

sound_spotlight.explanation: One flat inn with a doubled n, then the pronoun ending — no MSA anna, no vowel on the end. It leans onto the verb before it: aẕinn-innah.
A long aa before the final n, stressed. Add -a for a woman (zaʿlaana) and -iin for a group (zaʿlaaniin). Hearing the pattern lets you guess new ones: جوعان، عطشان، تعبان.
In Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE the feminine 'you' ending is ch, written ج or چ. Saudis keep -ik (رأيك). Both appear in this lesson's dialogue between two women.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second reaction clip: someone rates a restaurant or a phone. Listen for يعجبني / ما عجبني and the reason.
Nineteen words with audio; feeling adjectives show m / f / pl forms on tap.
Six faces, six words: مستانس، معصب، طفران، قلقان، زعلان، مرتاح. Audio only, then with text.
Drag أظن / أحس / قال + إن + a clause. Ten items, feedback highlights the pronoun ending.
Hear five opinions; reply with معك حق، بس… and your own view. Rubric: a softener before every disagreement.
Two-minute role play: الرياض ولا جدة؟ You must use بصراحة once and ما أوافق once, politely.
Word counter rolls up. Nudge: rate your dinner tonight in one Gulf sentence.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Rate the last thing you watched: بصراحة، أظن إن… and one feeling word for how it left you.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Activates the إن structure and a feeling adjective.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a friend وش رأيك؟ about anything today and reply to their answer with معك حق، بس…
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Real agreement-then-turn in conversation.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor one thing you hate and one you like about your city, and ask their opinion back.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor-session card. أكره / يعجبني plus a genuine exchange.

video_needs.scene: Two or three people giving opinions on a light topic — a restaurant, a car, a city — with أظن إن, بصراحة, معك حق and a visible mood word.
